Staging order is worth 8 GB: the dense blocks first with their host floats dropped between them, because 36 DeltaNet layers dequantise to 8.35 GB of transient f32 at once |
| [L5a](l5a-moe.md) | **The MoE block in Go — every tensor matched — and a routing distribution that is nothing like the uniform one everything was sized against.** 35.7% of the prefill graph and 97% of the parameters, checked against all fourteen nodes llama.cpp names in the FFN half at 4096 tokens: `ffn_out-3` at **1.378e-04 rms**, the three routed matmuls at 2.7-2.9e-03 (the *oracle's* fp16 accumulator, not ours), and `shared_expert_gate` at **4.152e-05** because one output column keeps it on the f32 vector path at any prompt length. The routing is the discrete half and the 4 k dump is the only place it can be checked: **0 of 40 960 slots differ as a set** on all 4096 tokens, and the two slots that differ in *order* are a pair the reference's own probabilities put **4.35e-07 apart relative** — so the test demands that any order disagreement be an unresolvable tie rather than demanding the order agree. Two findings that are not about correctness. **Modelling the reference's arithmetic makes the fit worse here, by 1.4-1.8x**: `Exact` f32 is 2.217e-03 against llama.cpp where `RefQ8` is 3.054e-03, where everywhere else in this vertical modelling the int8 activations was worth 233x (L2b-2), 69x (L2e-3), 2072x (L2e-2) or 2061x (L4a-6) — the reference has already lost eleven mantissa bits in the accumulator, so our quantisation error adds in quadrature rather than cancelling, and **L5b has nothing to reproduce**. And **the routing is not balanced**: L2a's budget assumed "each expert is read 10 times in 512" and the mean is the only part of that which holds — at ubatch 512 only **274 of 512 experts are touched**, the widest bucket is **484 tokens (95% of the ubatch)**, and **expert 454 is ranked first by 274 of the 512**, a second shared expert in all but name. Every bucket is cross-checked against llama.cpp's own `ffn_moe_topk`, so the skew is the model's: half the bank is read per ubatch rather than all of it, a workgroup-per-expert kernel has a **26x** imbalance that cannot be scheduled statically, and arithmetic intensity varies **484x** inside one dispatch. Three controls, because three things here have a plausible wrong version every tolerance passes: the expert bank read interleaved rather than expert-major (**175x** worse), `silu(up)*gate` for `silu(gate)*up` (**59x** — the narrowest, because silu is near-linear away from zero), and the `weights_sum` clamp, which guards a division by zero the data never reaches (smallest sum 0.0554 against 6.1e-05) and so is asserted from the graph rather than from the tensors |
| [L5b](l5b-moe-gpu.md) | **The MoE block on the device — the last kernel of the model, and the first one whose weights never become floats.** Nine dispatches against the ~845 llama.cpp spends on the same work: **567.4 ms of its 512-token prefill graph against 522.3, 1.09x**, and **1758.4 against 1131.6, 1.55x, at ubatch 2048** — with `ffn_out` at **8.132e-05 rms** over all 4096 tokens and the selection the reference's set for set *and order for order*. A layer's three expert banks are 5.03 GB as halves and 241 GB across the model, against 1.57 and 75 as they ship, so the bank is staged byte for byte and the kernel unpacks its own Q4_K/Q5_K/Q5_1/Q8_0 slab into LDS per K-step. **L5a-4's routing is what the schedule is:** 274 of 512 experts at ubatch 512 with one taking 95% of the tokens, so the tiles are a device-built *list* over a static bound rather than a grid — and every expert's rows are padded up to the row block so that a cooperative-matrix store, which covers sixteen rows and cannot be masked, can go straight to global; the slack is a **sentinel** row and poisoning it moves the output by exactly zero. Two optimisations worked and two did not, which is the point. Deleting the LDS epilogue is **1.35x** and widening the unpack's loads is **3.1x on Q8_0**; but sharing the dequantised slab across two or four waves of one workgroup — halving the unpack per row and doubling the waves a CU holds on a kernel running at one wave a SIMD — is **1.15-1.24x against**, and making the K-step cover a whole Q4_K nibble group, which removes a real 2x read amplification, is **1.16x against** because the doubled slab costs more occupancy than the reads cost bytes. The conflict-free LDS pad is **5.4x worse** than the four-way-conflicting one, because 16-byte row alignment is what the fragment load needs and every aligned pad conflicts. And two findings that are not about the MoE: the router is **bit-exact** against llama.cpp on all 2 097 152 logits where the CPU reference is at 3.6e-05, and so is `shared_expert_gate` — which **corrects L5a-1**, since `mul_mat_vec_max_cols` counts the columns of the *output*, so a [2560, 1] F32 weight is on the fp16 matrix cores at any real ubatch and fusing it onto the router costs nothing |
| [L4b](l4b-qsa-gpu.md) | **The QSA selection as a kernel — one dispatch where llama.cpp has twenty-four — and sparsity priced as a cost rather than a saving.** `llm_attn_select.comp` reads the per-cell scores `llm_attn_score.comp` already writes, radix-selects the threshold, and emits a **per-cell bitmask** rather than an index list — which deletes the `TOPK_QSA GET_ROWS` the reference spends turning one into the other. **2.40 ms of a 512-token graph becomes 1.24, 1.94x**, and 8.89 against 3.42 at ubatch 2048, **2.59x**; with the selection counted on both sides the full-attention layer is **68.8 ms against 29.6, 2.32x**, and 2.47x when `sparse` declines to run an identity the reference runs anyway. The optimisation is not where a radix histogram usually puts it: **the reference walks 256 buckets serially on lane 0** four times a row, and replacing that with a suffix sum plus an `atomicMax` is **1.86x** (192.0 → 103.3 us), while **per-wave histograms — the standard fix for LDS atomic contention — are 1.06x *against***. The cost side is the point: the selection makes the attention kernel **1.21x slower** for identical arithmetic (9950 → 12046 us at 4096 tokens), because every key block now passes through the P mask loop where only the diagonal did — and bit-testing the arena per element instead of staging the block's 16 mask words in LDS cost **1.90x**. Correctness is exact where it can be — the bitmask is `topK`'s selection **cell for cell on all 4096 rows** over the device's own scores, no tolerance — and 0.0381% of visible cells against llama.cpp's, **17x** L4a's CPU figure for a reason upstream of this kernel: **the indexer's two BF16 weights are fp16 column ranges of L2f-3's one fused matrix**, so the device cannot take L4a-6's bf16 activation and `indexer_k_raw` sits at 9.319e-04 — L4a-6's own *unmodelled* number — 2093x its modelled one, 24x on the score. It does not propagate: `attn_output-3` at 4096 tokens is **9.872e-04 rms**, inside the 1.14e-03 the same comparison gives at 7 tokens, and the dense control is **2.0x further**. Two traps the selection creates and the dense path cannot reach: `exp2(-inf - -inf)` is a NaN when a key block has nothing selected, and a pad row has no selection at all. And the attention ladder's **top two rungs invert with length** — qt2_kt4 overtakes qt1_kt4 at 4096 tokens — in the dense column too, so it is length and not sparsity; the winner does not move |
| [L4a](l4-qsa.md) | **The QSA selection reproduced exactly, and the oracle's arithmetic changing underneath it at a real ubatch.** The 7-token dump could test neither the selection (2051 cells asked of a 256-cell cache names every one) nor any tolerance (L3a-5's 8-column threshold puts it all on the f32 vector path), so a second dump: 4096 tokens, 4096 cells, one ubatch, 8.0 GB — which brings **the whole MoE block along for free**, so L5's fixture exists before L5 starts. The selection is `topk_radix_select.comp`, **a radix select and not a sort**: four 8-bit passes to the k-th key, emit everything strictly above, fill from the ties by `atomicAdd`. Ported pass for pass it reproduces `indexer_top_k` on **all 4096 rows** — and, unexpectedly, **set for set on the 2045 rows where the selection bites**, because filling the tie in ascending cell index is what a wave resolving an atomic in lane order does. A second dump pins the other half: byte-identical scores, an order that differs on **every** row, and a visible-cell set that differs on **none**. vLLM's block-granularity claim is now checked rather than read — 512 whole blocks + `(i+1) mod ratio` tail cells + a split of at most `ratio-1` cells off **the lowest-scoring block in the selection** — and run end to end from our own scores, **0.0022% of visible cells differ** (138 of 6.3 M, 30 of 4096 rows). Then the finding that was not about QSA at all: at 4096 columns **100% of every quantised matmul's output is exactly an IEEE half** — the coopmat `.f16acc` pipeline — for the DeltaNet's projections, the attention's, the MoE's and the shared expert's alike, while `hc_inject`, the router, `shared_expert_gate` and the BF16 indexer are 0%. So **the reference is the side losing precision at prefill**: three operand models (exact f32, fp16, the reference's own int8) land within **1.06x** of each other and all ~**5.4e-03 rms** away, and no chunked accumulator model improves it. The tolerance for a quantised projection at prefill is 5e-3, not the 1e-6 a 7-token dump suggests. And a fourth oracle numeric: the indexer's **BF16 weights meet a bf16 activation** above the threshold (`y_non_contig`), worth **2061x** on `indexer_k_raw` — with fp16 *worse* than f32, which is what makes it a different numeric from L2e-3's rather than the same one; L2e-3's fp16 F32xF32 matmul is separately **re-confirmed at 4096 columns**, 7.2x over f32. Two bugs fell out of the fp16 census, both in half-precision subnormals and both invisible to five stages of tensor comparison: `f16Round` returned **|x|** for every negative subnormal (`-0.0 + q*2^-24` is positive), and `f16` widened every subnormal to **half** its value (exponent field 113+e for 114+e) |
| [L3b](l3b-deltanet-gpu.md) | **The gated DeltaNet on the device — five dispatches where llama.cpp has eleven, and the scan-versus-chunk question answered by pricing it.** The lines of the reference's 512-token graph that are nameably this layer go from **152.8 ms to 111.5 — 1.37x, 13.1% of the whole graph becoming 9.6%** — with the recurrence itself at **413 us a layer against 438, 1.06x**. The fusion is L2a's again at a fourth site: `attn_qkv`, `attn_gate` and the two **F32** [2560, 48] gate projections read the same input, so they are one [16512, 2560] weight, and the 72 tiny-N F32 dispatches (7.8 ms a graph for 0.25 MB of weights at 1155 GFLOP/s) ride along free. That puts alpha and beta on the fp16 matrix cores — which is what **llama.cpp itself does at any ubatch past 8 columns** (L3a-5), so the deviation is from the 7-token dump and not from the reference; measured, it moves the log decay by 1.23e-03 rms and the per-token forgetting factor by at most **1.105%**. The scan's ladder is the finding: **LPC — how many lanes own one column of the [128, 128] state — sets the register count, the workgroup count and the operand re-read together**, and its two ends are **6.3x apart on identical arithmetic**. llama.cpp's own kernel is the top rung (6144 workgroups, a **128-fold** re-read of q and k, 2766 us), five rungs sit pinned at 1.18-1.31 TB/s while their flop rate varies 4x, and deleting the operand loads takes the widest rung from 2766 us to **1013** — so 63% of it is traffic it did not need. The winner is 16 state elements a lane and 768 workgroups. Registers beat LDS for the operands at LPC 8 and 16 and **lose by 1.33x at LPC 4**, where 96 registers a lane costs more occupancy than LDS costs latency — L2f-4's shape of result again. **And the chunked form is priced rather than built**: 1.15x the arithmetic on the matrix cores, a 4.3x ceiling and a realistic 1.1-1.6x, against a recurrence that is **13% of this layer where the fused projection is 64%** — a perfect chunked kernel saves 1.0% of the prefill graph and puts the recurrent state through fp16 operands |
| [L3](l3-deltanet.md) | **Gated DeltaNet — three quarters of the layers — in Go, against llama.cpp's own activations.** All eighteen tensors layer 0's graph names match: the recurrence's output to **3.11e-09 rms**, its 786 432-value state to **1.91e-08**, the layer's output to **1.31e-07**, and layers 1 and 2 with it. **The reference does not chunk**: `fused_gdn_ch` sends a multi-token batch to `ggml_gated_delta_net`, whose Vulkan kernel walks tokens one at a time with one workgroup per head — 438 us a layer at ubatch 512 — so `build_delta_net_chunking`'s 270 lines of `solve_tri` are a performance option and not the specification. Three things the architecture does not settle and the reference does: the **48 value heads read the 16 key heads by `h % 16` and not `h / 3`** (ggml's two broadcast rules disagree, they agree on 16 of 48, and the wrong one is **870 000x** worse); the **state is stored transposed**, so all three of a token's operations walk contiguous columns, which is why the kernel can keep it in registers; and **two things cross a batch boundary**, the recurrent state *and* the convolution's three-column window — 3+4 tokens reproduce 7 **bit-identically**. And the oracle turns out to be wrong about the model, not merely imprecise about the arithmetic: **the build behind this repo's trace, `PPL 4.0340` and `tg128 25.15` predates llama.cpp's "fix GDN normalization from `max` to `rsqrt`"** (#28068), and reproducing the bug is worth **15x** on the layer and 40x on the recurrence. Two more: L2e-3's "an F32 x F32 matmul is an fp16 matmul" is really a **dispatch threshold at 8 output columns** — so it is false for the 7-token dump's projections (86x the other way) and **will be true at a 512-token ubatch**, which every tolerance in L2 and L3 now depends on; and ggml's `softplus` adds in f32, so it flushes to **exactly zero** below -16.6 where `log1p` would be more accurate and wrong. **Cross-checked against vLLM**, which confirms the rsqrt normalisation, and whose **divide** head map is reconciled by llama.cpp's converter permuting the V heads into tiled order across seven tensor families — so `h % 16` is a fact about the GGUF, and **L8's bf16 path must replicate it or be wrong in 36 of 48 layers**. vLLM also **chunks for prefill** where llama.cpp scans, so L3b is a question two teams have split on |

`cmd/llm/bench_graph.go`: the five blocks in llama.cpp's own order, plus the
embedding gather and the head. [Write-up](research/l6b-graph.md) ·
`results/l6b_graph.csv` · `results/l6b_arena.csv`

> **L6b-1: it picks llama.cpp's token.** On the seven-token prompt the last
> token's argmax is **561** on both sides, and our top ten is llama.cpp's ten
> tokens — three adjacent pairs inverted, which is reported rather than
> demanded, because an inversion between logits a thousandth apart is a
> different fact from a wrong token. `result_norm` is **0.519% of scale** and
> `result_output` **1.983%**. **Nothing in a shader changed**: L6b is the
> order, the two tensors no block owned, and the plumbing.
>
> **L6b-2: three structural facts, all of them the reference's.** There is
> **no output norm** — `output_norm.weight` is absent and the final
> hyper-connection mixer is it, which makes `llm/gpu_head.go` the only bare
> matmul in the vertical. The **final mixer and the head run on one row**,
> because `inp_out_ids` drops every other token before them and the trace
> agrees: `result_output` is one row of 248320 floats for a seven-token
> prompt. And **the wide residual never leaves the mixer's arena** —
> `llm_hc_combine.comp` updates it in place — so what crosses a block
> boundary is the 2560-wide `hc_mixed` out and the 2560-wide block output
> back, not the 10240-wide stream.
>
> **L6b-3: the drift is a curve, and that is what makes 0.881% a number
> rather than a worry.** A second oracle pass filtered to `l_last` every
> eight layers, and the graph stopped at each depth off one staged model:
> **0.034 / 0.055 / 0.103 / 0.154 / 0.330 / 0.881% of scale at 8 / 16 / 24 /
> 32 / 40 / 48 layers** — a clean geometric **x1.085 a layer**, no step
> anywhere. That is what fp16 operands against the reference's int8 dot
> products (L2b-2) and its fp16 accumulators (L4a-5) compound to over 48
> residual additions. The four-layer prefix test prints the same column at
> depths 1-4 in 7 GB and three seconds.
>
> **L6b-4: the activation arenas were on the wrong memory type, and it was
> worth 5.0x.** The first working graph did **280.3 tok/s, 0.72x llama.cpp**,
> with 45.5% of its wall clock in plumbing that moves 5.24 MB a hop. The rate
> was the reason: the type `NewBuffer` prefers here is write-combined, and
> **the host reads it at 0.18 GB/s** where a HOST_CACHED type reads the same
> buffer at **25.06** and writes it 1.4x faster as well — **139x**, and
> DEVICE_LOCAL is one of the slow ones. **This is the other half of L0b**,
> which measured the same table from the *device* at 236.0-237.4 GB/s across
> all of it: free on the GPU, decisive on the host. The control says so

> **10834.5 us on cached arenas against 10850.2 on write-combined ones,
> 0.14%** — and is kept as `LLM_ARENA_UNCACHED=1` rather than as a note.
> Weight banks stay where they were: written once, never read.
>
> **L6b-5: the other half of the plumbing was the narrowing.** With cached
> arenas the glue is `Upload`'s f32→fp16 conversion — 1.31 M values a
> sublayer, 96 sublayers, **126 million a graph** — which was running on one
> core. The rows of a prefill are independent, so parallelising it changes
> the wall clock and not one value: **832 ms to 264** at ubatch 512.
>
> **L6b-6: the ladder inverts against the reference's.** 128 / 512 / 1024 /
> 2048 give **177.3 / 403.7 / 553.9 / 713.9 tok/s** where llama.cpp's own are
> 347.71 / 391.42 / 380.91 / 336.72: it peaks at 512 and **loses 14% by
> 2048**, because its 10240-wide F32 residual is 20.97 MB at 512 — just
> inside the 32 MiB MALL — and 83.9 MB at 2048 (L2a-4). Ours has no such

> the sublayer's, and one small narrowing kernel. L2a-3's projection for this
> graph with its glue fused was ~1150.

---

hardware. The measurements live in **`results/`, one CSV per op family**

sweeping everything by default. A run now has to name its targets:

files have always used, so keep it if they are to stay comparable row for

---
name: llm-resident-run
description: `go run ./cmd/llm -resident` stages the whole 84 GB qwen3.8-flash-next model; what it costs in time and RAM, and why nothing else can run beside it.
metadata:
  type: project
---

`go run ./cmd/llm -resident` (added 2026-09-16, LLM.md L6a) stages every layer
of all five blocks: **84.20 GB of device buffers, ~35 s wall clock**, and it
ends with about 41 GB of MemAvailable left on this 117.7 GiB machine. Peak
host memory is separate — the dense blocks dequantise to f32 before packing,
and the 36 DeltaNet layers are 8.35 GB of transient floats at once — which is
why the tool stages dense first and the 77 GB expert bank last.

**Why:** it is the only thing in the repo that takes most of the machine, so a
second GPU or large-allocation job started beside it will either fail to
allocate or perturb the timing it prints. `-bank N,N,...` restages just the
bank, which is the cheap way to vary residency; `-dense` is the 6.8 GB half
and runs in 8 s.

**How to apply:** run it in the foreground with a long timeout and nothing
else on the GPU, the way [[strix-halo-bench-runs]] asks. Its closing
measurement (layer 3's MoE block) is comparable to `-moe -tokens 512 -iters 10`
only at the same iteration count.

name: vulkan-mapped-arena-reads

Measured 2026-09-16 (LLM.md L6b, `results/l6b_arena.csv`,
`go test ./llm/ -run TestArenaMemoryTypes`): a mapped `VkBuffer` on this
machine is written at ~50 GB/s and **read at 0.18 GB/s** when it comes from a
write-combined memory type — which is what a plain "prefer DEVICE_LOCAL |

every type at 236-237 GB/s (LLM.md L0b), so the choice is free on the GPU.

whole graph** — 280 tok/s to 1400-equivalent — and it looked exactly like a

and `llm/arena.go`'s `newArena` exist because of it; `LLM_ARENA_UNCACHED=1` is
the control.

GPU timestamps, price a read of the arena before touching a shader. Use the
cached type for activation arenas the host reads; leave weight banks alone,
since they are written once and never read. Applies to the other verticals'
arenas too (`zimage/`, `parakeet/`) — none of them have been checked yet.

## What I built

**`llm/graph.go`** — the five blocks in `llama_model_qwen4exp::graph::graph`'s order over one staged model, plus `Prefill`/`PrefillN`/`Hidden`/`Forward` and a `GraphStats` that splits a pass into block and glue. `Layers: N` truncates it to a prefix so the order can be checked in 7 GB instead of 85.

**`llm/gpu_head.go`** — the one tensor no block owned. `output.weight` is [2560, 248320] Q8_0, staged a 4096-row slab at a time straight into the fragment tiling (never a 2.54 GB f32 copy), run as `llm_gemm.comp`'s MODE 2 on **one row** — because `inp_out_ids` is what the reference computes, and there is no output norm: the final hyper-connection mixer is it.

## The gate

Argmax **561** on both sides, out of llama.cpp's own top ten. `result_norm` 0.519% of scale, `result_output` 1.983%. I didn't just relax a tolerance to that — I dumped `l_last` every eight layers from the oracle and stopped the graph at each depth: **0.034 / 0.055 / 0.103 / 0.154 / 0.330 / 0.881%**, a clean geometric ×1.085 a layer with no step at any block, which is what fp16 operands against the reference's int8 dot products compound to over 48 residual additions.

## The finding

The first working graph was **280.3 tok/s, 0.72× llama.cpp**, with 45.5% of the wall clock in plumbing that moves 5.24 MB a hop. The rate was the reason, and it wasn't the memcpy rate: the memory type `NewBuffer` prefers here is write-combined, and **the host reads it at 0.18 GB/s** where a `HOST_CACHED` type reads the same buffer at **25.06** — 139×, with DEVICE_LOCAL among the slow ones. That's the other half of L0b, which measured the same table from the *device* at 236–237 GB/s across all of it. The control says it's free: the MoE block runs its layer in **10834.5 µs cached against 10850.2 write-combined, 0.14%**, kept as `LLM_ARENA_UNCACHED=1`. Parallelising `Upload`'s f32→fp16 narrowing (126 M conversions a graph, on one core) took the rest.

## The number

| tokens | tok/s | vs llama.cpp's 391.42 |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 128 | 177.3 | 0.45× |
| 512 | 403.7 (430.4 staged alone) | 1.03× (1.10×) |
| 1024 | 553.9 | 1.42× |
| **2048** | **713.9** | **1.82×** |

The ladder inverts against the reference's, which peaks at 512 and *loses* 14% by 2048 on L2a-4's MALL cliff — so against llama.cpp at the same ubatch it's **2.12×**.

`gofmt`/`vet`/`build` clean, `./llm/` and the zimage packages all pass. Written up in `research/l6b-graph.md`; `LLM.md`, `TODO.md` and the research index updated, and **L6c** added: the glue is still 22.7%, and the blocks alone already do **931.6 tok/s**.

<!-- LLM.md L6c. The glue between blocks moved from the host to the device:
     the move kernel, why it is not a shared arena, the fixed host cost that
     was hiding behind it, and the prefill ladder. Cited from llm/move.go,
     shaders/llm_move.comp, llm/graph.go and vk/engine.go. -->

[← LLM.md](../LLM.md) · [research index](README.md) · [L6b](l6b-graph.md) · [L2a](l2a-prefill-attribution.md) · phase 1

# L6c — the glue on the device: 941.3 tok/s, 2.40x llama.cpp

**Result: prefill is 941.3 tok/s at ubatch 2048 against llama.cpp's
best-of-any-ubatch 391.42 — 2.40x — and 572.9 at ubatch 512 against its 313.62
for the same 512-token prompt, 1.83x. Nothing crosses a block boundary through
the host any more, and not one number in the graph changed: `l_last` at all
six depths, `result_norm` and `result_output` are identical to the last digit.**

L6b left 22.7% of the graph in host plumbing. Every block here owns its own
four buffers, so an activation leaving one block and entering the next had to
cross a buffer boundary, and it crossed it by being read out of one mapped
arena, narrowed to halves on sixteen cores, and written into the other — 96
round trips a pass. This is that move as one dispatch.

| ubatch | L6b | L6c | | vs llama.cpp's 391.42 |
|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 128 | 177.3 | **259.0** | 1.46x | 0.66x |
| 512 | 403.7 | **570.4** | 1.41x | 1.46x |
| 1024 | 553.9 | **761.8** | 1.38x | 1.95x |
| **2048** | **713.9** | **941.3** | **1.32x** | **2.40x** |

Staged for 512 alone — a quarter of the arenas — ubatch 512 goes from 430.4 to
**572.9, 1.33x**. Two separate runs of the ladder agree to 0.54% at 128 tokens
and **0.01% at 2048**.

## L6c-1: the move, and why it is not a shared arena

`shaders/llm_move.comp` is three bindings and one loop: read floats from one
block's fp32 arena, write them into another block's arena as floats or as
halves. Bindings 1 and 2 are the *same* `VkBuffer` bound twice — a destination
is either an fp32 arena or an fp16 one, and a `narrow` push constant decides
which declaration the kernel writes through — so the two cases are one
pipeline shape rather than two shaders. A compute pipeline here owns its
descriptor set, so the host builds one per (source, destination) pair: **nine,
for the five blocks and the head**, on first use.

Each block exposes a `Port` for the two or three tensors that cross its
boundary and for nothing else, so what the graph may reach into is a short
list in each block's own file rather than an exported arena. A layer is then:

```
hc.Run(attn mixer)                          mixed, inject in the mixer's arena
move(sublayer.InPort()  <- hc.MixedPort())  f32 -> fp16, narrowed
sublayer.Run()
move(hc.BlockOutPort()  <- sublayer.OutPort())
hc.RunCombine(attn mixer)                   the residual, updated in place
```

**LLM.md's L6c said "one set of arenas", and this is not that.** Making the
five blocks bump-allocate out of one pair of buffers means splitting every
block's `alloc` into a pure layout pass and a materialisation — a descriptor
set needs its buffer before a pipeline exists, and a Vulkan buffer cannot grow
— which is a two-phase construction through five constructors and every caller
of them. The move costs what it costs instead, and L6c-2 says what that is.

## L6c-2: it is bit-exact, and it costs 2%

**Bit-exact.** Every figure L6b's gate prints came back identical to the last
place: `l_last` at 0.034 / 0.055 / 0.103 / 0.154 / 0.330 / 0.881% of scale at
8 through 48 layers, `result_norm` at 5.480e-01 rms, `result_output` at
3.144e-01, the same argmax out of the same top ten. That is the right outcome
and not an accident — `float16_t(v)` in SPIR-V and `safetensors.F32ToF16(v)`
in Go are the same round-to-nearest-even — and `TestMoveNarrow` is that claim
on its own: 37 rows of 2560 against the host narrowing **value for value**,
over halfway cases, subnormals and magnitudes past fp16's exact-integer range,
with the 27 pad rows zeroed and the A operand's pad *columns* untouched.

Those pad rows are not tidiness. The GEMM rungs have no bounds check, so the
rows between the prompt and the consumer's row block have to carry the
products of zeros, and a shorter run must not read what a longer one left
behind — which is why a destination `Port` states the row count it needs and
the move writes zeros up to it.

**And it costs 2%.** At ubatch 2048 the 197 moves a pass are **43.7 ms of
2175.8, 2.0%**, against the 22.7% of host plumbing they replace; at 128 tokens
they are 10.2 ms of 494.2, 2.1%. What is left on the host is 1.4-2.7%: the
embedding gather, the n-gram gather that D2 keeps off the device entirely, and
reading the logits back. **So a shared arena would buy that last 2% and
nothing else** — which is the measurement that turns "not built" into a
decision rather than a shortcut.

## L6c-3: the fixed host cost that was hiding behind the glue

With the moves in, the host column did something it should not: it **fell**
with the prompt length — 70.5 ms at 128 tokens, 61.3 at 512, 53.1 at 1024,
15.9 at 2048. Run the ladder backwards and the pattern follows the length and
not the position, so it is not a warm-up.

A cost that is flat per graph looks exactly like that. It was
`DeltaNetGPU.Reset`: the recurrent state is [128, 128, 48] f32 — **3.1 MB a
layer** — and a fresh sequence resets all 36 of them, spelled
`WriteFloat32At(off, make([]float32, StateSize()))`. That is **113 MB of Go
allocation a prefill**, zeroed by the runtime and then copied into a mapped
buffer that was about to be zeroed anyway. `vk.Buffer.ZeroFloat32At` clears the
mapping in place instead, and `HCGPU.UploadInit` writes `hc_init` — the
embedding repeated into four streams, 84 MB at ubatch 2048 — straight into the
residual arena rather than building the wide tensor on the host first.

| | 128 | 512 | 1024 | 2048 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| host, before | 70.5 ms | 61.3 | 53.1 | 15.9 |
| host, after | **11.1 ms** | **10.8** | **11.3** | **10.0** |
| tok/s | 226.8 → **259.0** | 533.8 → **570.4** | 731.1 → **761.8** | 932.2 → **941.3** |

Flat, as a fixed cost should be once it is only the logit read-back and the
`Resize` calls. It is worth **1.14x at 128 tokens and 1.01x at 2048**, and it
was invisible for as long as the glue around it was fifty times larger. The
same `WriteFloat32(make([]float32, n))` spelling appears in `zimage/dit`,
`zimage/vae`, `zimage/qwen` and `kokoro` — all of them at *allocation* time,
where it costs once and does not matter.

## L6c-4: where the 2048-token pass goes now

| | ms | % |
|---|---:|---:|
| moe | 1179.6 | 53.7 |
| deltanet | 446.4 | 20.3 |
| hyper-conn | 333.7 | 15.2 |
| attention | 137.3 | 6.3 |
| ple n-gram | 8.9 | 0.4 |
| lm head | 6.7 | 0.3 |
| move (device) | 43.7 | 2.0 |
| gather + host | 31.5 | 1.4 |

**96.6% of the graph is now the blocks** — 941.3 tok/s against the 974.9 they
would do with no plumbing at all. Against L2a-3's projection for this graph
with its glue fused (~1150) it is 82%, and the rest is inside the kernels:
L5b-7 already names the next 2.5x in the MoE as the unpack, and the DeltaNet's
fused input projection is 64% of that layer against the recurrence's 13%
(L3b-5).

**The short-prompt end is the honest weak spot.** At 128 tokens the MoE is
73% of the pass, because a routed expert bank costs what it costs to *read*
however few tokens are routed through it — the same reason llama.cpp's own
pp512 (313.62) is below its pp2048 (388.60). That is a decode problem wearing a
prefill hat, and it is L7's.
MD

session = '''### Session 2026-09-16 (forty-fourth) — stage L6c: the glue on the device, and 2.40x llama.cpp

**Result: prefill is 941.3 tok/s at ubatch 2048 against llama.cpp's
best-of-any-ubatch 391.42 — 2.40x — and 572.9 at ubatch 512 against
llama-bench's own pp512 of 313.62, 1.83x. Nothing crosses a block boundary
through the host any more, and not one number in the graph changed.**
[Write-up](research/l6c-moves.md) · `results/l6c_graph.csv` · `LLM.md`
rewritten.

**1. The move, and why it is not the shared arena the stage was scoped as.**
Every block owns its own four buffers, so an activation leaving one for the
next crossed a buffer boundary — and L6b crossed it through the host: read out
of one mapped arena, narrowed to halves on sixteen cores, written into the
other, 96 times a pass, 22.7% of the graph. `shaders/llm_move.comp` is that
move as one dispatch: three bindings, with **1 and 2 the same VkBuffer bound
twice** so that an fp32 destination and an fp16 one are one pipeline shape and
a `narrow` push constant rather than two shaders, and one pipeline per
(source, destination) pair — nine for the five blocks and the head. Each block
exposes a `Port` for the two or three tensors that cross its boundary and for
nothing else, so what the graph may reach into is a list in the block's own
file rather than an exported arena. **One shared arena across the five blocks
would need a two-phase construction through five constructors** — a descriptor
set needs its buffer before a pipeline exists and a Vulkan buffer cannot grow —
and L6c-3 prices what that would buy.

**2. It is bit-exact, and that is a test.** `l_last` at all six depths,
`result_norm` and `result_output` came back **identical to the last place**,
because `float16_t(v)` in SPIR-V and `safetensors.F32ToF16(v)` in Go are the
same round-to-nearest-even. `TestMoveNarrow` makes that a claim rather than an
observation: 37 rows of 2560 against the host narrowing value for value, over
halfway cases, subnormals and magnitudes past fp16's exact-integer range, with
the pad rows zeroed and the A operand's pad *columns* untouched. The pad rows
are load-bearing — the GEMM rungs have no bounds check, so the rows between the
prompt and the consumer's row block have to carry the products of zeros.

**3. And it costs 2.0%, which is what settles the shared arena.** The 197
moves of a 2048-token pass are **43.7 ms of 2175.8**, against the 22.7% of host
plumbing they replace; what is left on the host is 1.4% — the embedding
gather, the n-gram gather D2 keeps off the device, and the logit read-back. So
one set of arenas would buy that last 2.0% and nothing else, and it is written
down rather than built, the way L3b-5 answered scan versus chunk.

**4. A fixed host cost had been hiding behind fifty times its size.** With the
moves in, the host column **fell with the prompt length** — 70.5 ms at 128
tokens against 15.9 at 2048 — and running the ladder backwards showed it
follows the length, not the position, so it was not a warm-up. That is the
shape of a flat per-graph cost, and it was `DeltaNetGPU.Reset` spelled
`WriteFloat32At(off, make([]float32, n))`: the recurrent state is 3.1 MB a
layer and a fresh sequence resets 36 of them, so **113 MB of Go allocation a
prefill**, zeroed by the runtime and then copied into a mapping that was about
to be zeroed anyway. `vk.Buffer.ZeroFloat32At` clears it in place, and
`HCGPU.UploadInit` writes `hc_init` straight into the residual arena instead of
building its 84 MB on the host. The host column is now ~11 ms at every length,
worth **1.14x at 128 tokens**.

**5. The ladder.** 128 / 512 / 1024 / 2048 give **259.0 / 570.4 / 761.8 /
941.3 tok/s**, 1.32-1.46x on L6b at every length, with two separate runs
agreeing to 0.54% at 128 and **0.01% at 2048**. **96.6% of the graph is the
blocks now**: MoE 53.7%, DeltaNet 20.3%, hyper-connections 15.2%, attention
6.3%, moves 2.0%, host 1.4%.

**Next: L7, decode.** The short-prompt end is the honest weak spot — at 128
tokens the MoE is 73% of the pass, because an expert bank costs what it costs
to *read* however few tokens go through it, which is the same reason
llama.cpp's own pp512 sits below its pp2048. That is a decode problem wearing a
prefill hat. L2a-5 says decode is won by not dispatching 3837 kernels rather
than by a better GEMV, and L7 needs the KV cache ring, the indexer cache's own
incremental pooling, sampling and the generation loop.

'''
assert anchor in s
s = s.replace(anchor, session + anchor, 1)
open(p,'w').write(s)

content.text:
**L6c is closed — but not as the shared arena it was scoped as, and the measurement says why.**

## What I built

**`shaders/llm_move.comp` + `llm/move.go`** — the activation that crosses a block boundary, as one dispatch. Three bindings, with 1 and 2 the *same* `VkBuffer` bound twice so an fp32 destination and an fp16 one are one pipeline shape and a `narrow` push constant rather than two shaders. A pipeline owns its descriptor set here, so there's one per (source, destination) pair — nine for the five blocks and the head. Each block exposes a `Port` for the two or three tensors that leave it and nothing else, so what the graph may reach into is a list in the block's own file rather than an exported arena.

I did **not** build one shared arena. That needs a two-phase construction through five constructors — a descriptor set needs its buffer before a pipeline exists, and a Vulkan buffer can't grow — and the move costs **2.0% of the pass** against the 22.7% it replaces. So a shared arena would buy that 2% and nothing else; it's priced rather than built, the way L3b-5 answered scan-versus-chunk.

## Two results worth separating

**It's bit-exact.** Every figure of L6b's gate came back identical to the last place — `l_last` at all six depths, `result_norm`, `result_output`, the same argmax out of the same top ten — because SPIR-V's `float16_t(v)` and Go's `F32ToF16(v)` round the same way. `TestMoveNarrow` makes that a claim rather than an observation: 37 rows of 2560 value for value over halfway cases, subnormals and magnitudes past fp16's exact-integer range, with the pad rows zeroed (the GEMM rungs have no bounds check) and the A operand's pad *columns* untouched.

**And a fixed host cost had been hiding behind fifty times its size.** With the moves in, the host column *fell* with prompt length — 70.5 ms at 128 tokens against 15.9 at 2048. Running the ladder backwards showed it tracks the length, not the position, so not a warm-up; that's the shape of a flat per-graph cost. It was `DeltaNetGPU.Reset` spelled `WriteFloat32At(off, make([]float32, n))`: the recurrent state is 3.1 MB a layer and a fresh sequence resets 36 of them — **113 MB of Go allocation a prefill**, zeroed by the runtime and copied into a mapping about to be zeroed anyway. Clearing in place (plus writing `hc_init` straight into the residual arena instead of building its 84 MB host-side) flattens the host column to ~11 ms at every length; worth 1.14× at 128 tokens.

## The number

| ubatch | L6b | L6c | | vs llama.cpp's 391.42 |
|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|
| 128 | 177.3 | **259.0** | 1.46× | 0.66× |
| 512 | 403.7 | **570.4** | 1.41× | 1.46× |
| 1024 | 553.9 | **761.8** | 1.38× | 1.95× |
| **2048** | **713.9** | **941.3** | **1.32×** | **2.40×** |

Staged for 512 alone: 430.4 → **572.9**, which is 1.83× llama-bench's own pp512 of 313.62. Two separate ladder runs agree to 0.54% at 128 tokens and **0.01% at 2048**.

**96.6% of the graph is now the five blocks** — MoE 53.7%, DeltaNet 20.3%, hyper-connections 15.2%, attention 6.3%, moves 2.0%, host 1.4%. The short-prompt end is the honest weak spot: at 128 tokens the MoE is 73% of the pass, because an expert bank costs what it costs to *read* however few tokens go through it — the same reason llama.cpp's pp512 sits below its pp2048. That's a decode problem wearing a prefill hat, and it's L7's.

`gofmt`/`vet`/`build` clean; `./llm/`, `./gguf/` and all five `zimage` packages pass. Written up in `research/l6c-moves.md`, with `LLM.md`, `TODO.md`, the research index and `results/l6c_graph.csv` updated.
